A business is closed not because it fails but because it is “not on the right scale”. A career is wiped out by a door-slamming exit. People remember how they left, not what they did.
For someone living at the pole of inertia, the price is the mirror image — years. Time lived in a world that ended long ago.

sections.h2: How the 21-7-13 tail shows up in life
paragraphs: Below are typical scenes, not predictions. The tail describes a habitual course, not what is bound to happen.

paragraphs.h3: Relationships: The World stands at the entry twice

paragraphs: Point M — the entry of the tail — also serves as the entry of the relationship line M–R1–R. So for everyone with 21-7-13, the first card in closeness and the first card in the old scenario are the same — The World. Relationships begin with a picture of the whole: “us”, a shared home, a story forever. The conquest is the brightest phase: The Chariot knows how to win someone. Then the partner turns out to be a separate person with a life of their own, the scales start counting, and the couple ends either in a single evening or in a long cooling, when both spend years living in a petrified “us”.
The relationship line of this tail always begins with The World but never repeats the whole tail. In 21-7-13 the old scenario and the way of loving start from the same card and then go separate ways.
The strong version of this scene is a person who knows how to part humanely and is therefore not afraid to stay. When an ending stops being a catastrophe, there is no need to run.

Justice, Justice, The Tower. At work this often gives a rare ability — to close. Projects, divisions, loss-making branches, negotiations that drag on. Where others drag out for years what does not work, the person with this tail sees the end before anyone else and is not afraid to name it.

The shadow is the same ability without the scales. Firing someone “as a lesson to the rest”, shutting a project down a week before it pays off, breaking with a partner in the heat of the moment, walking out of a business at the cost of one’s share — anything to leave today. For 411 of the 678 people with this tail, or 61%, The Tower also stands in the social purpose — the point that shows how a person is useful to many; for the other 267 it is The Chariot. A repeated arcanum is not doubled by repetition, but it shows that in such a chart the theme of destruction and rebuilding goes beyond the tail, and its strong version can become a calling.

Popular readings advise this tail to take up professions that save lives: surgery, maternity wards, helping people in crisis. The cards give grounds for something broader — work in which ending is part of the job. Crisis management and restructuring, bankruptcy and winding up companies, editing where half the work is striking things out, rescue services, demolition and reconstruction, supporting people through divorce, inheritance and loss. Wen writes that Death is traditionally related to “death and birth, property and inheritance, society and family, war and treaties”. These are examples, not a prediction of a profession.

paragraphs.h3: Moving: a change of place as a way to end things

paragraphs: Waite’s divinatory list for The World contains words unexpected for a card of completion: **“voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”**. For 21-7-13 geography is part of the scenario. The fastest way to end everything at once is to leave: a new city, a new country, new people, and no one will ask how the past ended.

A move in this tail can be the completion of a chapter, or an escape from it. The difference is easy to see. Completion is when, before leaving, every word has been said, every debt paid and every task handed over. Escape is when the departure is the only word.

For a parent with this tail, a child growing up is the main exam, because childhood is an ending too, and the one that can least be cancelled. The Chariot wants to steer, and popular readings have good reason to advise this tail not to run their children’s lives. The loop can turn both ways here. One can cut: “if you’re so grown up, live on your own”, and shut the door on the day of the first serious argument. One can freeze: go on deciding for a thirty-year-old the way one decided for a ten-year-old, because the end of childhood was never acknowledged.
The version that works lies in between: notice that one stage has ended and say so out loud — in words, not with a slammed door.

sections.h2: Completion or destruction: telling them apart by the cards
paragraphs: The same card can work in two ways in this tail. The words in the table come from Waite’s divinatory lists and descriptions; the split into “loop” and “strength” is ours.

head: Card and role
When the loop is turning
When the strength is working
rows: “all or nothing”, flight and a change of place instead of a conversation; or fixity, stagnation
**assured success, recompense**: see it through and admit that it is done
war, presumption, vengeance; escape or rout instead of an honest confrontation
**succour, providence**: a will that carries others rather than crushing them
destruction, a break in a single evening; or inertia, petrifaction
**rebirth, renewal**: an ending with a road after it
a sentence passed in a private court, bias, excessive severity

paragraphs: Four questions help to see where a person is right now:

ul: **What is ending?** A person or a project — or only my picture of them?
**How long does the ending take?** One evening is a cut. Weeks with a conversation are a completion.
**Who heard about the ending?** Found out after the fact — a cut. Said face to face — a completion.
**What is left afterwards?** Scorched earth and blocked numbers — the loop. Meeting in the street and saying hello — The World.

sections.h2: What changes the scenario: nine practices
paragraphs: Waite’s horseman of Death **“moves slowly”**. Half the answer lies in that detail: an ending done well is not a blow but a passage that has time. Wen calls the appearance of Death “a call to let go of the present and move on” — to let go, not to destroy. The practices below add to the tail what The Chariot lacks: a pause, words and a voice at its back.

ol: **Get a voice at your back.** The Roman general in triumph heard “remember that you are a man”. What is needed is a person given the right in advance to say “stop” — a friend, a mentor, a partner. Any decision about a big ending — leaving, breaking up, closing a business — is first said out loud to them.

**Ride slowly.** A decision to end something, made today, is announced no sooner than a week later. If a week later it is the same, it is not a flare-up but a decision, and it can be carried out calmly.

**Separate the world from the picture.** Before the verdict, write down what exactly is wrong — the person themselves, the work itself, or the fact that they did not match my image? Many cuts end at this question.

**End with words.** Every ending comes with a conversation: what was good, what did not work, what I am taking with me. Even a short one. This is the “true, mature confrontation” that The Chariot, according to Wen, avoids.
**Listen for “he’s dead to me”.** It means the sentence has been passed without a defence. Replacing it with “we are no longer close” means ending without killing anyone.

**Hand things over.** When leaving a job, a project, a city — hand things over as if you might come back: pass them on, explain, say thank you. In Waite The World means “recompense”, and it goes to the one who saw things through.

**Clear one set of ruins.** Pick one burned bridge and complete it: a letter, a call, a returned debt, a “thank you” said at last. Not to restore it, but to close it. The bones of the horse are better buried than walked around.

**Set a deadline.** This is for the pole of inertia: set a date by which whatever is no longer alive will be either changed or ended — and keep it. The Chariot’s will in the service of Death, not against it.

**Celebrate completions.** Mark the ends of stages: a project delivered, a chapter closed, a child grown up. The World’s wreath is put on after the outcome, not before the battle. A victory without a celebration of completion quickly turns into the next war.

paragraphs: If thoughts of death stop being a metaphor — about your own life or someone else’s — that is not a question for the destiny matrix. In danger, call your local emergency number. Psychologists and crisis lines work with such thoughts, and you can turn to them at any moment.

sections.h2: The strong version of 21-7-13: the one who knows how to end wars
paragraphs: The tail holds a hint that only shows in Russian. Arcanum 21 is called Mir, and in Russian that word means both the universe and a life without war. Before the spelling reform of 1918 they were two different words: “міръ”, the universe or society, and “миръ”, the absence of war. Tolstoy titled his novel “Война и миръ”, War and Peace, setting peace against war; half a century later Mayakovsky answered with the poem “Война и міръ”, War and the World. The tarot card is mir in the first sense, the whole. But in 21-7-13 The World stands next to The Chariot, and in Waite’s list for The Chariot, right after “succour, providence”, comes “war”. War and mir meet in one triple — in both senses.

This is a play of the language, not Waite’s. But it describes the strong version of the tail exactly. Death, in Wen, is traditionally related among other things to “war and treaties”, and the end of a war is a treaty. **The strong 21-7-13 is not the one who never destroys, but the one who knows how to end wars — their own and other people’s.**

Such a person can be recognised by a few signs. They can close a project everyone is afraid to close — and do it so that people leave grateful. They leave without enmity and keep the doors open behind them. They finish what others abandoned halfway. In a crisis they calmly say “this is over” and lead people through the transition instead of running or smashing. They are not afraid of endings — so they need neither escape nor rout.

All of this is written in the same lists, only on the front side. For The World — **“Assured success, recompense”**. The list for The Chariot does not begin with war at all but with “Succour, providence”. For Justice — “Equity, rightness, probity”. And of Death Waite writes that its existing explanations — “rebirth, creation, destination, renewal” — are, on the whole, better than usual.

One last detail is about what the unarmed horseman carries. In Waite it is a black banner emblazoned with the Mystic Rose, and the rose, in his words, **“signifies life”**. Ahead, between two pillars on the verge of the horizon, shines the sun of immortality. Wen adds that the rider and horse are marching towards the rising sun, though that sun is still far in the distance. The path of 21-7-13 runs from an ending that cuts to an ending that carries the banner of life. The destroyer remains the same person with the same power to end things. What changes is only what is left behind: scorched earth — or peace.

sections.h2: How 21-7-13 differs from similar tails
paragraphs: Six other tails are easy to confuse with 21-7-13: they share the entry, the middle, the centre, or have Death among their cards.

head: Tail
Entry
Mechanism
Root
Centre
In common and the difference
rows: the same Chariot, the same centre and the same Manipura 8-8-16; a tail of beginnings, not endings
the same entry; The Chariot here is the root, not the mechanism
the same entry; power in the middle instead of motion
the same entry; The Tower at the root instead of Death
the same centre and the same Manipura 8-8-16
Death in the middle: the ending as a mechanism, not a task

paragraphs: The most instructive pair is 21-7-13 and 3-7-22. Both tails have The Chariot in the middle and Justice in the centre, and both have the same Manipura. But they drive in opposite directions. 3-7-22 is a tail of beginnings: from The Empress, who gives birth, to The Fool, who takes the first step. 21-7-13 is a tail of endings: from The World, where the road has been travelled, to Death. The same chariot carries some to the start and others to the finish.

Permutations — 13-7-21, 7-21-13, 21-13-7 and others — are never produced by the tail formula for any date. If such a triple turns up in a reading, it belongs to another position in the chart or to another school of calculation, and it cannot be read as 21-7-13.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation.** The classic destiny matrix by Natalia Ladini’s method: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M, with every sum reduced to 22 or below. The “sum of 13 or 49” rule and all the statistics come from going through every date from 01.01.1900 to 05.10.2026 — 46,299 days.

**Waite.** A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, 1922 reprint): the descriptions of The World, The Chariot, Death, Justice and The Tower from parts one and two, and the divinatory meanings from part three. Quotes are given in Waite’s original wording.
**Wen.** Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), the sections on The World, The Chariot, Death, Justice and The Tower. Quotes are given in Wen’s original wording.

**Literature and history.** A. S. Pushkin, “The Song of Wise Oleg” (1822), quoted in our translation; Tertullian, “Apology”, chapter 33; Plutarch, “On Tranquillity of Mind”, chapter 4, in the Loeb translation; the papal coronation rite with the words “Sic transit gloria mundi”, first recorded in 1409; L. N. Tolstoy, “War and Peace”; V. V. Mayakovsky, “War and the World” (1916).
**The Bible.** Ps. 127:1 (Ps. 126:1 in Russian numbering) — as the source of the verse Waite quotes.

**Our reading.** The three outcomes of an ending, the reading of the arithmetic (13 + 8 = 21, 13 + 21 → 7, 8 + 8 = 16), Oleg as a portrait of the loop and the play on the word “mir” are the author’s interpretation, not statements by Waite or Wen. The past-life legend is given as a popular interpretation, not as fact.

sections.h2: This tail in compatibility
paragraphs: In compatibility, 21-7-13 can be read as the task of changing a shared route in time while respecting different paces of adjustment. The World at M concerns ambitious plans and openness to new experiences; the Chariot at N develops the task through how goals are pursued; Death at D raises the question of ending an outgrown stage and accepting change. This is our interpretation using Lisovskaya’s pair positions, rather than a ready-made account from her book.

A shared venture may have stopped bringing satisfaction after many decisions were made for its sake. One person wants to close it; the other proposes simply working harder. The Chariot’s capacity to follow through can then keep the couple travelling a route that no longer serves their shared dream. The World helps reveal other possibilities, provided something new does not become a demand to erase everything that came before.

Name precisely what is ending: a particular project, a way of earning, or a familiar routine. Separate that from what you want to preserve between you, then divide the practical work of closing the stage. The difficulty is forcing a partner to change faster or treating every ending as defeat. A transition with clear steps helps this combination: acknowledge what has been done, settle commitments, and choose a small next experience that both people accept.

faq.q: What happened in a past life to someone with the 21-7-13 tail?
faq.a: The popular legend speaks of a cruel person who caused many deaths: an executioner, a jailer, a merciless fighter. This cannot be checked: a date of birth holds no information about past lives. The legend works as a metaphor for the scenario “conquer and destroy”, but not as a biography.

faq.q: Does Death in the tail mean an early death or danger to life?
faq.a: No. A calculated number says nothing about the length of a life or about misfortunes, and the threat of “leaving before your time if you don’t work off the tail” is intimidation, not method: there is no step in the calculation that would say so. Waite himself called the skeleton with a scythe a crude notion and considered the explanations “rebirth, renewal” better than usual. Death at the root of the tail is a task — learning to end things — not a forecast.

faq.q: Is the 21-7-13 tail different for women and men?
faq.a: The numbers are the same: sex plays no part in the calculation. Popular readings say that men with this tail travel a path from harshness to wisdom, while women go through scenarios of loss and submission. More likely the difference lies in what kind of ending people around allow: some are more easily forgiven a cut, others only long patience. The loop is the same either way: picture, victory, verdict, ending.

faq.q: Should someone with this tail become a surgeon or a rescuer?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The advice to “save lives” grew out of the legend of atonement. The cards of the tail speak of a different skill — ending things and leading people through a transition. A surgeon needs it, and so do a crisis manager, an editor and the parent of a teenager. The profession here is an example, not a prescription.

faq.q: What is the “21-7-13 programme”?
faq.a: That is sometimes what people call the karmic tail itself. This triple has no other place in the matrix: going through every date since 1900 shows that 21-7-13 never falls on the relationship line, the money line or the talent line, or in the chakras. If the triple is called a programme, it still means the tail.

faq.q: Can the 21-7-13 tail be “closed” or “worked off”?
faq.a: The numbers of a date do not change; the tail stays in the chart for good. What changes is how it is lived: the loop “victory — verdict — the cut” opens up when time and words appear between the decision and the ending. The measure is not a feeling of “I’ve worked through it” but the fact that one can calmly say hello to people from earlier chapters of life.

ul: **Cards and roles:** 21 The World — entry, 7 The Chariot — mechanism, 13 Death — root. Everyone with this tail has the same arcanum in the centre of the chart — 8, Justice.
**How to tell from a date:** the arcana of the day, month and year add up to 13 or 49. Both sums reduce to 13, and there is no other way to this tail.
**How often:** 678 dates out of 46,299 since 1900, or 1.46% — roughly one birthday in 68.
**The main trap:** not cruelty but an ending without a goodbye — sentence and break in a single evening.
**The way out:** end things slowly and all the way, so that every war is followed by peace.

report: Arthur Waite’s horseman of Death **“carries no visible weapon”**. Waite called the skeleton with a scythe “the crude notion of the reaping skeleton” and took it out of his deck. And yet the 21-7-13 tail, with this horseman at its root, goes by “the Destroyer and Killer” in popular readings.

A legend explains the name by a past life: the soul was supposedly an executioner, a jailer, a merciless fighter, and the cause of many deaths. None of this can be checked — a date of birth says nothing about past lives. Yet the vocabulary of the name really does lie in the cards. Waite’s divinatory list for Death opens with “End, mortality, destruction”. Among the meanings of The Chariot are “war, triumph, presumption, vengeance”. Only, what dies in this tail is not people but ties, projects and whole chapters of a life. A resignation letter written overnight. A move instead of a conversation. A number on the block list. And the phrase in which the tail is heard most clearly: “He’s dead to me.” That is the killing without a weapon.

report.h3: The King in his triumph and the death of Kings

report: Waite wrote down the link between the middle of the tail and its root himself. Of The Chariot he says: “it is really the King in his triumph”. Of Death: “more especially a card of the death of Kings”. The Romans joined the two long before tarot. Tertullian tells how a general riding in triumph was prompted from behind to look back and remember that he was only a man.

The Chariot itself does not hear that voice. Its conquests, in Waite’s words, are **“manifest or external and not within himself”**: it knows how to take the world from the outside, but on the inside nothing in it ever gets completed. Benebell Wen adds how such a victor ends things. He likes to appear in control, but tends to run from problems — or to attack them so hard that he subdues them and avoids “true, mature confrontation”. Escape or rout. Both bypass a third way — the conversation, the settling of accounts, the goodbye.

report.h3: Two endings, and a third that freezes

report: The tail opens with the card of the finale and closes with the card of the end. Waite calls The World “the perfection and end of the Cosmos” — the end as a summit: the work is done, the circle is closed. Death is the end as a break: the work is not finished, it has been stopped. Between them rides a victor.

There is a third outcome as well. In Waite, the reversed meanings of The World and of Death begin with the same word — “Inertia”: fixity, stagnation, petrifaction. When an ending can be neither completed nor broken off, it freezes. Hence the tail’s second pole: years in a job that has long been pointless and in a relationship where there has long been no one, and then everything torn down in a single day — including what was still alive.
The popular name sees only the break. But The World stands at the entry of the tail, which means that **the destroyer is the one who breaks off what could have been completed.**

report.h3: Oleg sent his horse away

report: The best portrait of this loop was written by Pushkin. “The Song of Wise Oleg” opens with the destroyer’s formula: the prince is setting out “to take revenge on the foolish Khazars” and has “doomed” their villages “to the sword and the fire”. Revenge, sentence, destruction. The prophecy runs exactly in the order of the tail: first The World — “The waves and the land bow down to thee”, then the horse that carries him to victory, and at the end — “But thy death shall come from thine own horse.”

Oleg does not argue with the ending. He cancels it: he dismounts and orders the horse to be led away. “And another horse was led up to the prince.” Years later the end catches up with him beside the bones of what he had sent away and forgotten. For 21-7-13, this is what matters most in the ballad: what has been removed from a life without being completed does not disappear — it lies on the hill and waits.

The loop turns like this. First comes a picture of the whole — what a family, a career, a project should be. Then victory: conquest comes to this tail more easily than anything. Then the crack: the conquered world is alive and does not match the picture. The scales switch on — everyone with this tail has Justice in the centre of the chart: “he brought it on himself”, “this is only fair”. The sentence is passed in a private court, with no defence. And the ending comes in a single evening. Then a new horse, the same picture ahead and new ruins behind. The price shows ten years on: no one is left from earlier chapters of life, and unfinished scenarios repeat themselves with new people.

report.h3: Mir, in both senses

report: The arithmetic of the tail points to the way out. The entry of the tail is the root plus the centre: 13 + 8 = 21. In our reading, Death laid on the scales gives The World. An ending that has been honestly weighed becomes a completion. And Waite’s horseman of Death **“moves slowly”**: an ending done well is not a blow but a passage that has time.

Hence the practices. Find a voice at one’s back — a person given the right in advance to say “stop”. Announce a decision about a big ending no sooner than a week later. End with words: what was good, what did not work, what I am taking with me. Listen for “he’s dead to me” and replace it with “we are no longer close”. Pick one burned bridge and close it — with a letter, a call, a returned debt. Not to restore it, but to close it.

The last hint only shows in Russian. Mir, the Russian name of arcanum 21, means both the universe and a life without war, and Waite’s list for The Chariot includes “war”. **The strong 21-7-13 is the one who knows how to end wars — their own and other people’s.** Such a person closes the project everyone is afraid to close, leaves without enmity, and leads people through a transition instead of running or smashing. In Waite the unarmed horseman carries a black banner with a rose, and the rose, in his words, “signifies life”. The destroyer remains the same person with the same power to end things. What changes is only what is left behind: scorched earth — or peace.

If thoughts of death stop being a metaphor — about one’s own life or someone else’s — this is not a question for the destiny matrix. In danger, call a local emergency number or crisis line; psychologists and crisis services work with such thoughts.

items.title: Karmic tail 3-13-10 in the destiny matrix: prune, don’t uproot

seo.title: 3 13 10 in the destiny matrix: a karmic tail without scare stories
seo.description: Tail 3-13-10: the Empress, Death and the Wheel. Why the “suicide” label is wrong, who has this tail, every birth date with it, and how to work with it.

items.short: The karmic tail 3-13-10 is the scenario of a gardener who grows living things generously, but at the first change of season doesn’t prune them — he pulls them up by the roots. The Empress at the entry (M) gives the desire to create, Death in the middle (N) turns every transition into a final ending, and the Wheel of Fortune at the root (D) teaches you to pass through a change of phase without losing the harvest. This is not a “suicide programme”, as popular lists frighteningly call this tail: it is about how a person ends projects and relationships, not about the end of life. The tail is rare — 149 birth dates since 1900 — and it always comes with the centre 20, Judgement.

sections.h2: In short: what 3-13-10 means

head: Point
Arcanum
Role in the tail
How it sounds in 3-13-10
rows: the desire to grow something living: a business, a relationship, a home, a team
a transition is lived as a complete ending; after the break comes relief
to pass through a change of phase and carry experience into the next round
E — centre (not part of the tail)
the decision “that’s it, enough” comes as a revelation, and so it feels right

paragraphs: If you boil it down to one thought: Death in this tail is not a misfortune that befalls what was created, but the habitual way a person closes stages themselves. Working through the tail does not mean you stop ending things. It teaches you to end a part, not the whole.

sections.h2: Why 3-13-10 is called “Suicide”, and what is wrong with that label
paragraphs: In popular lists, the 3-13-10 tail is labelled “Suicide” or “the Suicide”. Then usually come stories about a soul that “failed to cope in a past life”, about a weak instinct for self-preservation and a choice “between life and death”. The label is put together mechanically: the Empress is life, Death is death, the Wheel is fate, so the total is “a life cut short by one’s own hand”. If you have come here after such a reading — especially a reading of your child’s chart — breathe out. This conclusion does not follow from the arcana themselves.

In The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Arthur Edward Waite writes of the thirteenth card as change of form and passage “from lower to higher”. On his horseman’s banner is the Mystic Rose, “which signifies life”, and between the pillars on the horizon shines “the sun of immortality”. He finds the existing explanations of the card better than usual on the whole: “rebirth, creation, destination, renewal”. Waite does not strike the theme of death out of the card, but neither his book nor Benebell Wen’s modern Holistic Tarot gives any grounds for predicting death or misfortune from the arcanum. And a karmic tail in the Arcana Sense scheme does not assign events at all: it describes a habitual pattern that repeats.

The frightening label does have an honest grain of truth, and it is worth naming directly. This scenario has a difficult place — the pause between the end of one form and the start of the next. The old is already over, the new not yet planted, and the empty field can feel heavy: “I don’t feel like doing anything”, “it was all for nothing”. This is not a sentence and not a character trait but a phase, discussed in detail below.

If thoughts of death are not a symbol from the matrix but something that is happening to you or someone close to you right now, you need to talk to a living person, not to the arcana. Call your local emergency number or a local crisis line — crisis lines talk to children, teenagers and parents too.

sections.h2: The scenario: grow, uproot, start again
paragraphs: Waite calls the Empress the door or gate by which an entrance is obtained into this life, and an image of universal fecundity: a field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water. In the 3-13-10 tail she stands precisely at the entry. So the circle begins not with a problem but with a rise: an idea, a person, a project, a home appears — and you want to grow all of it. Such a person starts out of desire, not duty. People and resources gather quickly around their idea, and the first fruits appear sooner than other people’s.

Then the season changes. There is nothing catastrophic about this; it is how all living things live: a project needs rules and a different scale, falling in love needs agreements, a grown child needs a different distance, a team needs new roles. At such a moment a gardener prunes branches, moves the plant to a bigger pot, thins something out. In the weak version of 3-13-10 a different reflex kicks in: if the old form no longer fits, then everything is over. And the plant is pulled up by the roots.

Then the Wheel turns and a new season comes: a new field, a new idea, a new rise. The person is generous again, grows things fast again — and at the next change of form again puts a full stop where a comma would have done. After a few turns a familiar feeling appears: “everything starts beautifully for me and always ends the same way”. Wen writes of the Wheel as a card under which history repeats itself and the past becomes the future, down to a sense of déjà vu. For this tail, déjà vu is the most accurate signal that the circle has started another turn.

paragraphs.h3: What uprooting looks like, and what repotting looks like

head: Where
How the tail works
What the way out looks like
rows: close the project when it has outgrown the “garage” format and needs procedures
change the format: hire people, delegate, keep the product and the clients
quit as soon as the role changes or a new manager arrives
discuss the new role and bring into it what you did best
break up when falling in love gives way to everyday life
rework the agreements on time, money, duties and intimacy
quietly disappear from a group that has changed
change how often you meet and keep the people you still feel warmly about
abandon and delete a piece that you’ve “stopped liking”
finish the series, set the draft aside, start the next part
move and start from scratch, giving things away, instead of renovating
remake the space for a new stage of life

paragraphs: There is neither cowardice nor whim in the left-hand column. There is decisiveness that has mistaken a stage for the whole.

sections.h2: What keeps the circle going: relief that feels like a revelation
paragraphs: Death in position N is the mechanism that makes the repetition stable. Its mature work is to end what has outlived itself and free up space. In the tail this work is overdone: instead of one dry branch, the whole tree goes. And things immediately feel easier. You don’t have to endure the in-between stage, where the old no longer works and the new has not yet taken shape. You don’t have to watch a beautiful beginning turn into a complex system. Relief fixes the circle in place more reliably than any belief. Wen herself links Death with the darker aspects of the Wheel of Fortune: change you don’t control and a transition you resist.

3-13-10 has a second support too, invisible if you look only at the tail’s three numbers. This tail only arises with a matrix centre of 20 — Judgement (how this works is explained in the section on arithmetic). Waite describes Judgement as a response to a call heard from within: something in us sounds a trumpet, and all that is lower rises in response — “almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye”. Wen calls this card an epiphany: all the evidence is on the table, the judgement has been made.

In our reading, it is this link that explains why the break in 3-13-10 doesn’t look like running away. The person doesn’t slip off into something new, as in the neighbouring tails with the same entry — they pass a verdict. The decision “that’s it, enough” comes all at once, feels like clarity, almost like an awakening, and so seems unconditionally right. Sometimes it really is right. But the feeling of revelation doesn’t prove the verdict correct: the trumpet can sound out of tiredness, too, or out of fear of the transition. Time helps to tell one from the other — more on this in the practical part.

sections.h2: The second trap: numbness after the ending
paragraphs: In Waite’s list of divinatory meanings, the thirteenth card has “end … destruction”, and reversed, “inertia, sleep, lethargy”. A calculated number has no reversed position, but the pair itself is telling: a transition can be failed in two ways — by cutting it off too early, or by getting stuck after the end. In her reading of the reversed card, Wen describes the second option as a plateau: the person feels it is time to move into a new phase and cannot budge.

In 3-13-10, numbness often follows the break. The garden has been uprooted, the field is empty, and a new desire has not yet come. The Empress is the ability to want and to grow, so the empty field is felt especially sharply: a person used to living from one idea to the next suddenly wants nothing. This, apparently, is where the gloomy interpretations of the tail come from.

The Wheel at the root gives a direct answer: winter is a phase, not the end of the garden. “What goes up will come down. What hits bottom will bounce up,” Wen writes of the tenth arcanum. It helps the holder of 3-13-10 to know a simple thing about themselves: emptiness after an ending happens to them, and it passes. It doesn’t have to be filled at once with a new start, and it shouldn’t be taken as the truth about life. If it drags on and grows heavier, that is a reason to talk to a psychologist, not to look for answers in the matrix.

sections.h2: The root task: stay on the wheel instead of jumping off
paragraphs: Position D is the root task the whole circle keeps returning to. Here stands the Wheel of Fortune. Waite sees in it the perpetual motion of the world and the flux of human life, and in the sphinx at the top of the wheel, the equilibrium within this motion. He specifically notes that seating the sphinx on a fixed pedestal above the wheel spoils the symbol: the meaning of the card is stability amidst movement, not apart from it. And one more of his thoughts: behind the turns of the wheel stands not chance but Providence.

For 3-13-10 this is a ready-made statement of the task. You can’t stop the wheel: the Empress will grow things anyway, and what grows will change form anyway. Jumping off at every turn, as the tail’s Death does, is no way out either. The task is to become someone who stays themselves while the forms change: “this form is over, but the story goes on”. Then the experience of the previous round passes into the next one instead of burning up with the old shell.

In practice, the Wheel teaches you to tell phases apart. Any living undertaking has sowing, growth, a plateau, pruning and winter. A plateau is a pause in growth, not its end. Pruning is care for the tree. Winter is not emptiness for ever. A person with 3-13-10 most often mistakes two difficult but ordinary phases for the end — the plateau and the pruning. Learning to name the phase out loud is already half the work.

sections.h2: How to prune instead of uprooting: practice
paragraphs: The ability to put a full stop is a strength of this tail, and there is no need to give it up. The task is narrower: to end stages, not everything at once. Below are six techniques, each answering a specific link in the circle.

What exactly has stopped working? What of what you have created is still valuable? What next form could it move into? If all three questions have concrete answers, the decision looks like pruning. If there is only one answer — “I want this to be gone” — it is most likely relief talking, not clarity.

Before any ending, write down what you are taking with you: skills, people, money, texts, groundwork, conclusions. The Empress does not grow things so that everything burns. If the inventory comes out empty, you are probably leaving too early: the harvest hasn’t been gathered yet.

A decision to end things comes as a revelation, so let it sit. Say it out loud to someone you trust, set a date and come back to it in a few days. Real clarity will survive the pause; a rush of relief usually won’t.
Find the smallest ending that will relieve the tension: close one role, one format, one commitment, one project out of five. Often this is enough for the tree to start growing again.

When a stage really is exhausted, end it completely: say thank you, hand things over, settle debts and agreements, say goodbye. A break leaves things unsaid, and it is exactly from that unsaid that the numbness after the ending grows. A good ending is Death in its mature form: a horseman with a rose on his banner, not an explosion.

When the feeling “this has happened before” appears in a new situation, stop. This is the place where the circle repeats and where it is easiest to break: make at least one move on this turn differently from the previous ones.

sections.h2: Arithmetic and rarity: what sets 3-13-10 apart among the 26 tails
paragraphs: In the Arcana Sense scheme, the tail is calculated like this: D is the reduced sum of the day, month and year arcana, the centre E is the sum of all four, then M = D + E and N = D + M. Any number over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. For 3-13-10 the arithmetic adds up to an almost narrative picture: the Wheel and Judgement give the Empress (10 + 20 = 30, reduced to 3), and the Wheel and the Empress give Death (10 + 3 = 13). Death in the middle is literally the sum of the root and the entry.

This can be read as a hint — as our interpretation, not a rule of the method. Death here is not an outside force that takes away what you created. It is made of two of your own qualities: what you grow, and the fact that every living thing goes through phases. The meeting of growth with a change of season is inevitable; the only choice is whether it becomes pruning or uprooting.

Add the day arcanum (numbers up to 22 are taken as they are; for 23–31, the sum of the digits), the number of the month and the year arcanum (the sum of the digits of the year; if over 22, add the digits again). If you get exactly 10, your tail is 3-13-10. If you get 28, 37, 46 or 55, the Wheel also stands at the bottom of your chart, but the tail is different: 21-4-10. For example, 4 January 1949: 4 + 1 + 5 (1 + 9 + 4 + 9 = 23, then 2 + 3) = 10.

A sum of exactly 10 requires all three terms to be small, so the tail is rare. From 1 January 1900 to the start of October 2026, 149 dates out of 46,298 give it — 0.32%. That makes it the third rarest of the 26 tails the formula produces; only 9-18-9 and 6-14-8 are rarer. The 21-4-10 tail also has the root 10, and it is about 27 times more common.

Two more features follow from this. The 3-13-10 tail only occurs in people born between 1 January and 1 July. And more than half of the matching dates — 88 of 149 — fall in 2000–2024. There are no such dates at all before 1949, and after 1 January 2024 the next one will not come until 4 January 2030.

paragraphs.h3: What always stands next to 3-13-10 in the chart

paragraphs: Everyone with this tail has the same sum of day, month and year, so several more points match for all of them. They are a handy way to check that the chart has been calculated correctly.

head: Point
Value for everyone with the 3-13-10 tail

paragraphs: There is also a match that does not apply to everyone. For those born in 1949, 1958, 1967, 1976, 1985, 1994, 2003, 2012 and 2021 (45 dates of 149), the same numbers 3-13-10 also stand on the relationship line. This is not a doubled force of the tail but two different positions, each with its own reading: the theme “grow it and don’t cut it off” also sounds in the reading of their close relationships.

sections.h2: 3-13-10 in a child: what parents should know
paragraphs: More than half of the dates with this tail fall in the 2000s, 2010s and 2020s. So people often learn about 3-13-10 while calculating a son’s or daughter’s matrix, and immediately stumble on the word “suicide”. Let us repeat the main point: the tail says nothing about a child’s safety and does not predict events. It describes a way of going through transitions that in childhood is only just taking shape.

It might look like this. A child lights up over a club, a sport, a friendship, a project of their own, throws themselves into it generously and with pleasure — and at the first turn (a new coach, a different class, a first serious failure) wants to drop everything for good. In the logic of the tail, this is not a whim but the same Death, only on a child’s scale.

What helps is a middle path between two extremes: don’t force them to hold on to everything, and don’t let them burn everything at once. Agree to “finish the season” before leaving. Ask not “why are you giving up” but “what from this do you want to keep”. Show by your own example how to end things well: say goodbye, say thank you, take your skills with you. The most valuable thing a child with 3-13-10 can take away from childhood is the experience that after one stage ends, they remain the same person, with everything they managed to grow.

If what worries you is not the matrix but what you see in your child’s mood and behaviour, that is a question for real specialists. Call your local emergency number or a local crisis line — crisis lines advise parents too.

sections.h2: Similar triples: how not to confuse 3-13-10
paragraphs: Tails that share one number are easy to take for relatives. But in a tail, what matters is the number’s role, not the number itself, so their scenarios are different.

head: Tail
What it shares with 3-13-10
How it differs
rows: centre 11 instead of 20: the person answers the turn of the wheel not with a break but with an attempt to hold everything through control
the home grows walls, and the person breaks out by force — or takes everyone under control
stops at the threshold: a new start seems more interesting than the plan that is due to come into the world

paragraphs: Against their background, 3-13-10 stands out because it doesn’t run away but ends things: it passes a verdict and puts a final full stop.

The same three numbers also occur elsewhere in the chart — and there they are no longer a karmic tail but the programme of another line, with its own reading. Most often it is the personal talent line: the 3-13-10 triple stands there for people born in March with centre 7, and there are almost three times as many such dates since 1900 (431) as dates with the tail. Less often it is the relationship line (110 dates, 45 of them belonging to holders of the tail themselves). By the formula, this triple never occurs in the money line.

In the Arcana Sense formula there is no such tail as 10-13-3. If you have seen it in someone else’s reading, most likely the same points have simply been written in reverse order — from the outer bottom point to the inner one. Check against your chart: you have the 3-13-10 tail if 3 is at the inner bottom point, 13 in the middle and 10 at the outer bottom point. In the compatibility matrix the numbers are calculated from two dates, and the 3-13-10 triple there describes the couple, not each partner’s personal tail.

sections.h2: The strong version: a gardener who knows the seasons
paragraphs: A worked-through 3-13-10 gives a rare combination: the ability to create living things from scratch, the courage to clear away what has outlived itself without needless regret, and the understanding that both are parts of one long cycle. Such people are good at taking projects and people through transitions: relaunching projects, moving teams to a new format, helping others close a chapter well without losing what mattered most in it. Where others cling to the shell or throw everything away along with it, they know how to repot.

The difference between the weak and the strong version shows after the ending. The weak one leaves relief, an empty field and a vague déjà vu. The strong one leaves a gathered harvest, a clear conclusion and a next move that builds on what has been lived. The Empress grows, Death prunes, the Wheel turns the season, and Judgement at the centre sounds no longer like a verdict but like a call to the next form of life.

sections.h2: This tail in compatibility
paragraphs: In a pair matrix, 3-13-10 concerns growing something shared when familiar conditions change. The Empress at M connects to the wish for comfort and tangible results; Death at N develops the task through letting go of what no longer fits; the Wheel of Fortune at D draws attention to shared steadiness across changing stages. This connection is our reading of Lisovskaya’s pair roles, rather than a ready-made meaning for the triple in her book.

Suppose the household routine no longer fits the partners’ work schedules. One tries to preserve every ritual; the other proposes cancelling them all. Behind an argument about dinner time may be a more precise question: how can care remain without repeating a form that has become burdensome? The Empress establishes the value of what you create; Death helps release that value from an old form; the Wheel asks the couple to learn to revisit arrangements without feeling the entire relationship is collapsing each time.

Choose one habit together and design a replacement for the next two weeks. Instead of an elaborate dinner every day, for instance, agree on a simple breakfast together and one shared evening. The difficulty is waiting for ideal conditions to return, or dismissing earlier effort as pointless. Check whether the care both people need has survived in the new arrangement, then adjust it together based on what you find.

faq.q: Is the karmic tail 3-13-10 really “Suicide”?
faq.a: No. That is a popular label assembled from a literal reading: the Empress is life, Death is death. Waite interprets the thirteenth arcanum as change of form and renewal, and a karmic tail describes a habitual scenario, not events. 3-13-10 is about how a person ends projects and relationships: too abruptly, all at once and with relief.

faq.q: How rare is the 3-13-10 tail?
faq.a: It is the third rarest of the 26 possible tails: 149 birth dates since 1900, 0.32%. It only arises if the day, month and year arcana add up to exactly 10. That is why all such dates fall between 1 January and 1 July, and more than half of them in 2000–2024.

faq.q: Is the 3-13-10 tail linked to children, pregnancy or motherhood?
faq.a: The Empress is an image of fertility, but neither Waite nor Wen gives any grounds for predicting pregnancy, childlessness or the loss of a child from her. In this tail she means the ability to grow any living undertaking: a project, a relationship, a home, a team. Readings that link 3-13-10 to abortions or “maternal trauma” go beyond what the cards say.

faq.q: How is 3-13-10 different from 21-4-10?
faq.a: Both tails have the Wheel of Fortune at the root, but their centres differ: for 3-13-10 it is Judgement (20), for 21-4-10 it is Strength (11). Hence their opposite answers to the turn of the wheel: 3-13-10 ends everything too early, 21-4-10 holds on to everything too tightly. 21-4-10 is about 27 times more common.

faq.q: How do I know the tail has been worked through?
faq.a: By what remains after the ending. If after every ending you have a gathered harvest — people, skills, conclusions — and your next step builds on the previous round instead of starting from zero, the scenario is working in its strong version. The second sign is that you can end one stage without destroying the whole project or the whole relationship.

faq.q: Can I get rid of the 3-13-10 karmic tail?
faq.a: The numbers of the chart don’t change: they are calculated from your date of birth. What changes is how the scenario works. The goal is not for the tail to disappear, but for its Death to prune rather than uproot, and for every new turn of the Wheel to begin with the harvest of the last one.
